location.value: Anatolia in West Asia and East Thrace in Southeast Europe. Capital Ankara, and largest city Istanbul.

terrain.value: A mountainous plateau ringed by Black Sea, Aegean and Mediterranean coasts, controlling the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits. Area 783,562 km².

climate.value: Mediterranean on the coasts, continental inland.

resources.value: Farmland, minerals (chromium, boron), hydroelectric power, and tourism.

disasters.value: Major earthquakes: İzmit (1999) and the 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquakes (about 59,000–62,000 deaths in total).

urbanisation.value: Rapid urbanisation. Istanbul is one of the world’s largest cities.

disease.value: COVID-19 (2020–22). Not otherwise detailed in the sources checked.

migration.value: The Greek–Turkish population exchange (1923). Labour migration to Germany from the 1960s. Turkey hosts millions of Syrian refugees (since 2011).

economicBase.value: An upper-middle-income economy: industry, services, agriculture and tourism.

tradeRoutes.value: A bridge between Europe and Asia. Major trade with the EU (customs union, 1995).

wealth.value: GDP about $1.82 trillion nominal ($21,079 per person) and $4.03 trillion PPP (2026 estimates, Wikipedia infobox).

moneyAndTax.value: The Turkish lira, which has gone through periods of very high inflation (e.g. the 1990s and the 2020s).

governmentType.value: A unitary presidential republic (since the 2017 referendum). Officially a secular state with a Muslim-majority population.

keyRulers.value: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (president 1923–1938). İsmet İnönü. Adnan Menderes. Turgut Özal. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (prime minister from 2003, president from 2014).

succession.value: Elections, with a multi-party system since 1950, interrupted by military interventions.

institutions.value: The Grand National Assembly. The 1924 and 1982 constitutions. Secular reforms: the abolition of the caliphate (1924), the Latin alphabet (1928), and women’s right to vote nationally (1934).

stability.value: Military coups or interventions in 1960, 1971, 1980 and 1997, a failed coup attempt in 2016, and a long conflict with the PKK (a ceasefire in 2025).

eliteConflict.value: Tension between secularist and religious-conservative elites, and between the military and elected governments.

armyAndTech.value: One of NATO’s largest armies (NATO member since 1952), with a growing domestic arms industry (drones).

majorWars.value: The Turkish War of Independence (1919–1923). The Korean War (1950–53). The intervention in Cyprus (1974). The PKK conflict (from 1984).

territoryChange.value: Borders set by the Treaty of Lausanne (1923), and Hatay added in 1939.

alliancesRivals.value: A NATO member and EU candidate (accession talks since 2005). Tensions with Greece, Cyprus, Armenia and at times the EU and US.

inventions.value: Infrastructure megaprojects (bridges, the Marmaray tunnel), and a defence and drone industry.

scienceEducation.value: Secular national education (from 1924), the alphabet reform, and mass literacy campaigns.

openness.value: Westernising reforms under Atatürk, and EU integration efforts. Concerns about press freedom have grown since the 2010s.

religion.value: Officially secular, with a Muslim-majority population (mostly Sunni, with a large Alevi minority). Religion share figures are not given in the infobox.

languageWriting.value: Turkish (official), in the Latin alphabet since 1928. Kurdish, Zaza, Arabic and others are spoken. About 70–75% Turkish and 19% Kurdish (2016).

artsArchitecture.value: Ottoman heritage (Istanbul’s mosques), modern Turkish literature (Orhan Pamuk, Nobel Prize 2006), music and cinema.

socialStructure.value: Diverse urban and rural society. Women gained the vote in 1934. There are tensions over Kurdish rights.

sharedIdentity.value: Turkish nationalism (Kemalism) founded on the republic’s 1923 reforms. Debates over secularism, religion and Kurdish identity.

neighbours.value: Greece, Bulgaria, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran, Iraq and Syria.

ideasReligions.value: A model of a secular Muslim-majority state in the 20th century.

colonisation.value: The successor of the Ottoman Empire. Wikipedia states the Ottomans committed genocides against Armenians, Greeks and Assyrians during WWI; the Turkish government rejects the genocide characterisation.

riseSignals.value: Victory in the War of Independence and Atatürk’s sweeping reforms (1920s–30s).

peakPeriod.value: Ongoing: rapid economic growth in the 2000s.

declineSignals.value: Not in decline. Challenges named in the sources include inflation, democratic backsliding, the Kurdish conflict, and refugees.

outcome.value: Ongoing: a presidential republic, NATO member and upper-middle-income economy.

sources.value: Official statistics and modern histories. Checked against Wikipedia (“Turkey”) on 6 Nov 2026. See also Zürcher (2017).

overallCertainty.value: High for statistics. Recent politics and historical questions (the Armenian genocide) are contested, so this entry uses the sources’ own wording.
